cards.back: Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. Only at Full Moon. Anyone on the night side of Earth can see it; in totality the Moon turns red.
The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, and the Moon's shadow falls on Earth. Only at New Moon. The shadow is small, so only a narrow path sees it total.

Umbra: the dark center of the shadow, all of the Sun blocked: total. Penumbra: part of the Sun blocked: partial. Antumbra: beyond the tip of the umbra, the Moon looks smaller than the Sun and leaves a ring: annular.

cards.back: The plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun. From Earth it is the Sun's path through the stars over the year; the planets stay close to it.

cards.front: Inclination of the Moon's orbit to the ecliptic
cards.back: $i = 5^\circ$. The Moon's orbit is tipped 5° to the ecliptic, so it is usually a little above or below the Sun–Earth line.

cards.front: Why don't we see a lunar eclipse every Full Moon?
cards.back: The 5° tilt. Most months the Full Moon passes above or below Earth's shadow, and the New Moon's shadow misses Earth. Only when New or Full lands where the Moon crosses the ecliptic do we get eclipses: an eclipse season.

cards.back: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$ · $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$ · $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}$. The hypotenuse is across from the right angle; opposite and adjacent are named from $\theta$.

cards.front: Trig example: solve for an unknown side
cards.back: Hypotenuse 8, angle 25°, find the opposite side. Opp and hyp → SOH: $\sin 25^\circ = \dfrac{x}{8}$, so $x = 8\sin 25^\circ = 3.38$. Calculator in degree mode.

cards.front: Trig example: solve for an unknown angle
cards.back: Opposite 3, adjacent 5. Opp and adj → TOA: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{5}$, so $\theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) = 31.0^\circ$. Use the inverse button ($\tan^{-1}$).

questions.stem: A lunar eclipse can only happen at which phase?
choices: New
First Quarter
Full
Third Quarter
questions.explain: Earth has to be between the Sun and the Moon, with the Moon on the far side from the Sun: Full.

choices: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
the Moon's shadow falls on Earth
the Sun's light is blocked by Earth's atmosphere
the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun
questions.explain: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth (New Moon) and its shadow lands on a small patch of Earth.

questions.stem: The Moon's orbit is tilted to the ecliptic by about
questions.explain: $i = 5^\circ$. (23.5° is the tilt of Earth's axis, a different thing.)

choices: the Moon's path around Earth
the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun
the line between day and night on the Moon
the shadow of Earth on the Moon
questions.explain: The ecliptic is the plane of Earth's orbit; from Earth it is the Sun's yearly path through the stars.

questions.stem: The Sun is {t}° above the horizon. How long is the shadow of a {h} m flagpole?
questions.explain: The pole is opposite the angle and the shadow is adjacent → TOA: $\tan {t}^\circ = \dfrac{{h}}{x}$, so $x = \dfrac{{h}}{\tan {t}^\circ} =$ {answer} m. Lower Sun, longer shadow.

questions.stem: You see a ring of the Sun around the Moon: an annular eclipse. Which part of the Moon's shadow are you in?
choices: Umbra
Penumbra
Antumbra
Earth's shadow
questions.explain: The antumbra lies past the tip of the umbra. From there the Moon looks a little smaller than the Sun and leaves a ring of fire.

questions.stem: Why isn't there a lunar eclipse every Full Moon?
choices: The Moon is too far away from Earth
The Moon's orbit is tilted 5°, so the Full Moon usually passes above or below Earth's shadow
Earth's shadow is too small to reach the Moon
The Sun is not always behind Earth at Full Moon
questions.explain: The 5° tilt. Only when Full Moon happens near where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic does it pass through Earth's shadow.

questions.stem: Who can see a total lunar eclipse?
choices: Only people in a narrow path about 100 miles wide
Anyone on the night side of Earth with a clear sky
Only people at the equator
Only people where it is daytime
questions.explain: The Moon itself goes dark, so everyone who can see the Moon sees it. A total solar eclipse is different: the Moon's small shadow makes a narrow path.

questions.stem: There is a solar eclipse today. When is the next chance for a lunar eclipse?
choices: Tonight
In about 2 weeks, at the next Full Moon
In about 6 months
In about 18 years
questions.explain: We are in an eclipse season, when the Moon is near the ecliptic. The next Full Moon is half a cycle later, $\tfrac{29.5}{2} \approx 15$ days, so it often passes through Earth's shadow too.

questions.stem: Put what you see during a total solar eclipse in order.
items: The Moon takes a growing bite out of the Sun (partial)
Baily's beads: the last sunlight shines through valleys on the Moon's edge
Totality: the corona shines around the black Moon
Beads again on the other edge
Partial again as the Moon moves off
questions.explain: Partial, beads, totality with the corona (glasses off only now), beads on the far edge, then partial again.

questions.stem: Why are some solar eclipses annular instead of total?
choices: The Moon is farther from Earth than usual and looks a little smaller than the Sun
The Sun is closer than usual
Earth's atmosphere bends the light
It happens at Full Moon instead of New
questions.explain: The Moon's distance changes over its orbit. When it is far, it doesn't quite cover the Sun, and Earth sits in the antumbra: a ring of fire.
